newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia bonds drop, no longer sure on rates.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia bonds drop, no longer sure on rates.

text.p: *The Australian debt market came under severe pressure after the RBA's quarterly bulletin left the market far from clear that official interest rates will be eased again.
*Short-end hardest hit having been pricing in a 50 b.p. cut.

The Australian debt market came under severe selling pressure after the Reserve Bank's Bulletin left the market far from certain that an official interest rate cut will be endorse when the board meets on November 5.
The short-end was particularly hit, having been pricing in a 50 basis point easing in current 7.0 percent rates.

The RBA said in its September quarter report, in its October bulletin, that low inflation expectations support the case for an easing, and would strengthen if the economy proves weaker than expected, but a cut does depend on wages growth.

"What this (the Bulletin) has done has shown the market that it's not a dead certainty that we are going to see a rate cut. The market had been quite confident that there would be before," said Andrew Ticehurst, economist at Macquarie Bank.

However, he noted that the Bulletin had been finalised on October 8 and since then the market has seen a weak business survey by the National Australia Bank, a weak labour market report, and another sharp fall in consumer sentiment.
The October Westpac consumer sentiment index released today showed a further 3.9 percent fall, and has now dropped 9.2 percent since its peak in March to its lowest level in a year.
The December bill futures contract tumbled to 93.37 after the RBA report, indicating a cash rate of 6.63 percent, having touched a high of 93.56 on Wednesday.
Long bond yields also rose back over 7.70 percent after brushing 7.50 percent yesterday.

"It's really showing fair value at the long end of the curve. We are at the trough of economic growth and from here on you would expect things to be picking up somewhat, and that's where 7.50 (percent) is a bit of a barrier," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

Bond yield spreads blew out sharply against other dollar bloc bonds after the RBA release. The Australian/U.S. 10-year spread widened to its highest level in over 2-1/2 weeks, while it went to a premium over the long end of the New Zealand market for the first time since end-July.

The technical outlook for the 10-year bond contract has turned negative after breaching 92.330, but should find some support at the pyschological 92.250. Market now awaits U.S. bond market reaction to the U.S. September CPI later today.
